## Proof

**Claim.** There exists a monotone (increasing) function $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ whose set of discontinuity points has cardinality $\aleph_0$.

**Construction.** Let $\{q_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ be an enumeration of $\mathbb{Q}\cap(0,1)$. Define the Heaviside function $H:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ by $H(t)=1$ if $t>0$ and $H(t)=0$ if $t\le 0$. Set
$$
f(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^n}\,H(x-q_n),\qquad x\in[0,1].
$$

**The series is well defined and $f$ is bounded.** Since $0\le H(x-q_n)\le 1$ and $\sum_{n}2^{-n}=1$, the series converges absolutely and uniformly by the Weierstrass $M$-test, with $0\le f(x)\le 1$.

**$f$ is monotone increasing.** Each summand $x\mapsto 2^{-n}H(x-q_n)$ is non-decreasing, and a uniformly convergent series of non-decreasing functions is non-decreasing. Hence $f$ is non-decreasing on $[0,1]$.

**$f$ is discontinuous at every $q_k\in\mathbb{Q}\cap(0,1)$.** Fix $k$. For any $x<q_k$ we have $H(x-q_k)=0$, while for any $x>q_k$ we have $H(x-q_k)=1$. Therefore
$$
f(q_k)-f(x)\;\ge\;\frac{1}{2^k}\bigl(H(q_k-q_k)-H(x-q_k)\bigr)\;=\;\frac{1}{2^k}\bigl(0-0\bigr)=0\quad(x<q_k),
$$
and more usefully, for $x<q_k<y$,
$$
f(y)-f(x)\;\ge\;\frac{1}{2^k}\bigl(H(y-q_k)-H(x-q_k)\bigr)=\frac{1}{2^k}>0.
$$
Letting $x\uparrow q_k$ and $y\downarrow q_k$ gives $f(q_k^+)-f(q_k^-)\ge 2^{-k}>0$. Thus $f$ has a jump of size at least $2^{-k}$ at $q_k$, so $f$ is discontinuous at $q_k$.

**$f$ is continuous at every irrational $x\in(0,1)$.** Since $f$ is monotone, the one-sided limits $f(x^-)$ and $f(x^+)$ exist, and discontinuity at $x$ is equivalent to $f(x^+)-f(x^-)>0$. We estimate, for $\varepsilon>0$,
$$
f(x+\varepsilon)-f(x-\varepsilon)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^n}\Bigl[H(x+\varepsilon-q_n)-H(x-\varepsilon-q_n)\Bigr].
$$
The bracketed term equals $1$ exactly when $x-\varepsilon<q_n<x+\varepsilon$ (up to the harmless boundary cases $q_n=x\pm\varepsilon$, which contribute at most two terms and vanish in the limit), and equals $0$ otherwise. Hence
$$
f(x+\varepsilon)-f(x-\varepsilon)\;\le\;\sum_{\substack{n\,:\,q_n\in(x-\varepsilon,\,x+\varepsilon)}}\frac{1}{2^n}\;+\;\text{(boundary terms)}.
$$
Now fix any $N$. Since $x$ is irrational, $x\ne q_n$ for every $n$, so for each $n\le N$ there exists $\varepsilon_n>0$ with $q_n\notin(x-\varepsilon_n,x+\varepsilon_n)$. Taking $\varepsilon<\min_{n\le N}\varepsilon_n$, none of $q_1,\dots,q_N$ lies in $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)$, so
$$
f(x+\varepsilon)-f(x-\varepsilon)\;\le\;\sum_{n>N}\frac{1}{2^n}\;=\;\frac{1}{2^{N}}.
$$
(The boundary terms also vanish as $\varepsilon\to0$ since $x$ is not of the form $q_n\pm\varepsilon$ for fixed $n$ in the limit; rigorously, for $\varepsilon$ small enough the interval endpoints avoid all $q_n$ with $n\le N$.) Since $N$ is arbitrary,
$$
f(x^+)-f(x^-)=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}\bigl[f(x+\varepsilon)-f(x-\varepsilon)\bigr]\;\le\;\frac{1}{2^N}\quad\text{for every }N,
$$
which forces $f(x^+)-f(x^-)=0$. Thus $f$ is continuous at $x$.

**Conclusion.** The set of discontinuities of $f$ is exactly $\mathbb{Q}\cap(0,1)$, which is countably infinite, i.e. of cardinality $\aleph_0$.

Therefore, **yes**, such a monotone function exists. $\blacksquare$
